title: When you're ill
hook: sickness is not punishment; Jesus healed the sick
tomorrow: Abuela's hands have hurt for years. why did nobody know?

segments.voice: That was a week of days that come back: remembered days, your first birthday, your saint's day, faith you can taste, once a year. Yesterday's line: a few days apart. Now a new stretch begins, about suffering and hope.
screen: `A FEW DAYS APART.` → `THE DAYS THAT COME BACK.` → `SUFFERING, AND HOPE.`

segments.voice: A fever, the very week you were supposed to shine. Lying on the couch, it's tempting to do the math: what did I do to deserve this? Skipped something, said something, owed somebody? Jesus's own friends did that math out loud, about a man born blind. And Jesus refused to show his work their way.
screen: `A FEVER, THIS WEEK OF ALL WEEKS.` → `WHAT DID I DO?` → `THE FRIENDS DO THE MATH.`

segments.voice: John tells it. The disciples see the man and ask, in the Douay-Rheims: "Rabbi, who hath sinned, this man, or his parents, that he should be born blind?" Two choices, both blame. Jesus picks neither: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents; but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." Then he spits on the ground, makes clay, puts it on the man's eyes, and sends him to wash. One to tell a friend: the pool is called Siloe, and John stops to tell you the name means sent. The man comes back seeing. So the Church keeps a sacrament just for the sick, the anointing of the sick, from the letter of James: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him." Illness here isn't a verdict. It's a place where God's works can still show up, through healing, through a doctor, through the people on the couch beside you. And every day of last week still holds when you're ill: a remembered day, a first birthday, a few days apart.
screen: `WHO HATH SINNED?` · `NEITHER.` · `CLAY, WATER, SIGHT.` · `ANOINTING OF THE SICK.` · then, large: `NOT A PUNISHMENT.`

segments.voice: Put one hand over a place that hurts or feels tired, or over your heart if nothing does. Breathe slowly there, and let the question of blame go quiet. If you pray, you can pray for your own health, plainly, the way you'd ask for anything you need.
When you're ill. The time Catholics are taught to meet not as a punishment but as a place God can still work. Today's word.
Keep this one: not a punishment, neither this man nor his parents. Get some rest.
